cells.source:
# Custom connector

Cells run top to bottom in a fresh process on every execution -- there is no
persistent kernel, so state is rebuilt from these cells each time.

This notebook must define `test_connection()` and `extract()`. It may also
define `discover()` and `fetch_content(asset_id)`.

Configuration comes from `ctx`:

- `ctx.var("name")` -- a value from **Variables**
- `ctx.secret("name")` -- a value from **Secrets** (encrypted, redacted from output)
- `ctx.strategy` / `ctx.limit` / `ctx.offset` -- this run's sampling. Every
  strategy works without you doing anything; pushing these into your own query
  just makes it cheaper. Under LATEST, "latest" means whatever you yield first.
  Reading `ctx.offset` means you apply it yourself and the runtime stops skipping.
- `ctx.should_abort` -- check it in long loops so Stop can work.
from classifyre import Asset, ctx

def extract():
    """Yield Asset(...) objects. Runs on every scan."""
    yield Asset(
        id="example-1",
        name="Example record",
        url="https://example.com/records/1",
        content="Hello from a custom connector.",
        kind="record",
        metadata={"origin": "scaffold"},
    )

CUSTOM.name: REST API with a bearer token
CUSTOM.description: Pages a JSON API, reading the base URL from a variable and the token from an encrypted secret. Related ticket ids become asset links.

cells.source: from classifyre import Asset, ctx

def extract():
    session = requests.Session()
    session.headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {ctx.secret('api_token')}"

    page = 1
    while not ctx.should_abort:
        payload = session.get(
            f"{ctx.var('api_base')}/tickets",
            params={"page": page, "per_page": 100},
            timeout=30,
        ).json()
        if not payload["items"]:
            return

        for item in payload["items"]:
            yield Asset(
                id=str(item["id"]),
                name=item["subject"],
                url=f"{ctx.var('api_base')}/tickets/{item['id']}",
                content=item["body"],
                kind="document",
                metadata={"status": item["status"], "assignee": item["assignee"]},
                links=[str(related) for related in item.get("related_ids", [])],
            )

        page += 1

CUSTOM.name: Parse files of any format
CUSTOM.description: Turns a PDF, image, spreadsheet or JSON payload into text with parse(), the same parser every built-in source uses. Keeps the raw bytes on the asset so the image and binary detectors see the real file.

cells.source:
# Parsing files

`parse()` takes a path, raw bytes, an open handle or a file from `ctx.files`,
works out what it is, and extracts its text. PDF, DOCX, XLSX, PPTX, ODF, EML,
MSG, RTF, HTML, JSON, CSV, Parquet, archives and images all go through it, and
an image or a scanned PDF is OCR'd.

It never raises: a corrupt file comes back with `.error` set and empty text, so
one bad attachment costs one asset rather than the run.

Two fields, and why you want both:

- `content=` is the text detectors read.
- `content_bytes=` is the file itself. Set it and the image, binary and
  file-metadata detectors work too, and the asset keeps its real MIME type.

For something too large to hold whole -- a Parquet dump, a million-line CSV --
use `pages()` instead and emit an asset per page.
from classifyre import Asset, ctx, pages, parse

def extract():
    """One asset per file, with both its text and its bytes."""
    for file in ctx.files:
        parsed = file.parse()
        if parsed.error:
            # Worth recording rather than skipping: a file that cannot be read
            # is a fact about the source, not an absence.
            ctx.log(f"could not parse {file.name}: {parsed.error}")
            continue

        yield Asset(
            id=file.name,
            name=file.name,
            kind="file",
            content=parsed.text,
            # The bytes, so the image/binary detectors run against the real file
            # rather than against extracted text.
            content_bytes=file.read_bytes(),
            mime_type=parsed.mime_type,
            metadata={"size_bytes": file.size_bytes},
        )

cells.source:
# Uploaded files

Upload files to this source in the form above and they arrive as `ctx.files`.

They are downloaded to local disk before any cell runs, so each one is an
ordinary path:

- `ctx.files` -- every file, ordered by name
- `ctx.file("dump.csv")` -- one by name
- `file.path` / `file.open()` / `file.read_bytes()` / `file.read_text()`
- `file.parse()` -- text extraction for any format
- `file.pages()` -- read it a page at a time instead of whole

This is the mechanism to use in a Kubernetes deployment: the runner is an
ephemeral pod with no filesystem of yours to reach, so files travel with the
source. You can also point at a folder instead -- see the
"Read a mounted folder" template.
from classifyre import Asset, ctx

def extract_one_known_file():
    """When the connector expects a particular file rather than all of them.

    `ctx.file(...)` raises with the names that *are* there, so a renamed upload
    is a clear message rather than an empty scan.
    """
    manifest = ctx.file("manifest.json")
    for line in manifest.read_text().splitlines():
        yield Asset(id=line, content=line)

CUSTOM.name: Read a mounted folder
CUSTOM.description: Walks a folder configured on the source and turns each file into an asset. Works in both deployments: a path on this computer on desktop, or a volume mounted into scan pods by the chart in Kubernetes.

cells.source:
# A folder the scan can read

Add a folder in **Files & folders** above and reach it with `ctx.folder("name")`,
which hands back a `pathlib.Path`. Nothing is copied: the notebook opens the
files where they are, which is what makes this workable for a dump too large to
upload.

The path is resolved on the machine that runs the scan. On desktop that is this
computer, so any path you can open works. In Kubernetes it is an ephemeral scan
pod, so the folder has to be mounted into CLI jobs first -- set
`api.localFolders` in the chart, then enter the `mountPath` you gave it (for
example `/mnt/corpora/dumps`).

If you would rather not mount anything, upload the files to the source and read
them with `ctx.files` instead.

from pathlib import Path

from classifyre import Asset, ctx, parse

#: Everything else in the folder is skipped rather than guessed at.
WANTED_SUFFIXES = {".json", ".csv", ".txt", ".log", ".pdf", ".docx", ".xlsx"}


def extract():
    root = ctx.folder("dumps")
    for path in sorted(root.rglob("*")):
        # A walk over a real folder can run for a long time, and Python cannot
        # be interrupted from outside -- this check is what makes Stop work.
        if ctx.should_abort:
            return
        if not path.is_file() or path.suffix.lower() not in WANTED_SUFFIXES:
            continue

        parsed = parse(path)
        if parsed.error:
            ctx.log(f"skipping {path.name}: {parsed.error}")
            continue

        relative = path.relative_to(root)
        yield Asset(
            # Relative to the folder, so moving the folder does not orphan every
            # asset and its findings.
            id=str(relative),
            name=path.name,
            url=path.as_uri(),
            kind="file",
            content=parsed.text,
            content_bytes=path.read_bytes(),
            mime_type=parsed.mime_type,
            metadata={"size_bytes": path.stat().st_size, "folder": str(relative.parent)},
        )

CUSTOM.name: Linked assets
CUSTOM.description: Emits assets that reference each other -- a ticket and its attachments, a document and the records it cites -- so the graph shows how they connect.

cells.source:
# Linking assets to each other

`Asset.links` holds the ids of *other assets this notebook yields*. Those
become edges in the graph, and they are what lets a finding on one asset be read
in the context of the others.

Use the ids you assign, not hashes or URLs -- the runtime resolves them:

    yield Asset(id="ticket-1", links=["attachment-1", "attachment-2"])
    yield Asset(id="attachment-1", ...)

Order does not matter: a link to an asset yielded later resolves fine. A link to
an id this run never yields simply has nothing on the other end.

Links are directional as written. Link both ways when both directions are worth
following.
from classifyre import Asset, ctx

def test_connection() -> dict:
    return {"status": "SUCCESS", "message": "Ready."}

#: Stand-in for whatever you actually read from. Replace with your own client.
TICKETS = [
    {
        "id": "SUP-1041",
        "title": "Refund request",
        "body": "Customer asked for a refund on order 88213.",
        "attachments": [
            {"id": "SUP-1041-a1", "name": "receipt.txt", "body": "Order 88213 - $240.00"},
        ],
        "related": ["SUP-1039"],
    },
    {
        "id": "SUP-1039",
        "title": "Duplicate charge",
        "body": "Charged twice for order 88213.",
        "attachments": [],
        "related": [],
    },
]


def extract():
    for ticket in TICKETS:
        if ctx.should_abort:
            return

        attachment_ids = [item["id"] for item in ticket["attachments"]]
        yield Asset(
            id=ticket["id"],
            name=ticket["title"],
            kind="document",
            content=ticket["body"],
            # Both its own attachments and the tickets it references. These are
            # this notebook's ids; the runtime turns them into graph edges.
            links=[*attachment_ids, *ticket["related"]],
            metadata={"external_id": ticket["id"]},
        )

        for attachment in ticket["attachments"]:
            yield Asset(
                id=attachment["id"],
                name=attachment["name"],
                kind="file",
                content=attachment["body"],
                # Linked back, so the edge is followable from either end.
                links=[ticket["id"]],
                metadata={"parent_ticket": ticket["id"]},
            )
